thinking: Detailed Phase 1-5 structural scan for SoCal housing market analysis. Stated claim sensationalizes transactional lows as a total economic crash; ground reality shows a severe affordability and inventory freeze with elevated prices.
subject: Home buying crashes in SoCal with levels worse than Great Recession
posts:
Home sales across six Southern California counties plunged 33% below historical averages, hitting transaction lows worse than the Great Recession.
Evidence: Attom data, Jonathan Lansner analysis
#RealEstate #SoCal #Economy

Analysis frames the drop as an unprecedented market collapse driven by high mortgage rates and record-high home prices.
Stated Judgement: (-0.60, +0.70) — Greatest Lie

While sales volume is severely depressed, median prices remain near record highs ($815k+), indicating an affordability freeze rather than a destructive price crash.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.30, -0.30) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Revelation into Destruction.
Sensationalizing transactional volume as a price crash obscures the reality of sticky valuations and high borrowing costs.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.8, z: 1)
A Southern California buyer faces an estimated monthly payment of $5,765—a 72% increase over five years—making renting far more viable.

The Bright Side:
Price growth has slowed to manageable single digits, preventing runaway appreciation from locking out future buyers entirely.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHO (prospective buyers priced out) with WHAT (transaction volume vs property values), fueling sensational clickbait.

SocialPhysics Analysis:
Media outlets run a smart selfish loop, packaging macro interest rate freezes as an apocalyptic crash to harvest clicks from anxious consumers.

The Trajectory: The Path of Revelation into Destruction.
Mapping depressed transaction volume against stubborn price floors yields a neutral-negative stagnation vector. ΔH = 0.5.

The Unavoidable Truth: High mortgage rates and soaring costs have locked out the vast majority of Southern California households.

The Unavoidable Lie: Property values are actively collapsing across the region like in 2008.

Alethekanon:
Low transaction volume equals a frozen market, not a price crash. Terminology matters when describing economic strain.

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreakingly hard for young families to save enough for a down payment when monthly costs have nearly doubled.

Brothekanon:
Sales are dead because rates are high, but sellers aren't dropping prices. It's a standoff, not a crash.

Spirithekanon:
"He who loves money will not be satisfied with money." Ecclesiastes 5:10 PASS
When shelter becomes speculative extraction, communities freeze in place.

aspects.reason: Accurate sales data framed with sensational crash terms.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Home buying crashes in SoCal with levels worse than Great Recession

Across six Southern California counties, home sales in the 12 months ending in July were 33% below the average annual pace recorded since 2005, according to an analysis from Los Angeles Daily News business columnist Jonathan Lansner

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Homebuying in Southern California has slowed to a pace even worse than during the Great Recession, with sales nearing historic lows while prices remain close to record highs.

Attom, a real estate data firm, recently revised its home sales figures dating back to 2005, using new methods to identify actual transactions in public records.

Los Angeles Daily News business columnist Jonathan Lansner analyzed the figures through July 2026 and found that home sales remain incredibly low, while buyers who manage to close deals are paying near-record prices.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Never miss a story

The updated data includes sales of both existing and newly built houses and condos.

Across six Southern California counties, home sales in the 12 months ending in July were 33% below the average annual pace recorded since 2005.

Lansner’s analysis found that this was the second-slowest 12-month period for home sales in more than two decades, surpassed only by May 2026.

Perhaps even more striking, July’s sales pace was 3% slower than during the worst stretch of the housing market collapse in the late 2000s.

Southern California’s housing market has been struggling for three years, with home sales falling to levels rarely seen in more than two decades.

Of the 25 months with the fewest home sales over the past 21 years, 17 have occurred since 2023. Seven took place during the 2007-2008 financial crisis, while another came in May 2020, when pandemic restrictions brought much of the economy to a halt.

The slowdown comes as homeownership remains unaffordable for much of Southern California. High prices, elevated mortgage rates and uncertainty surrounding the local economy have discouraged prospective buyers, many of whom are finding that renting is a far less expensive option.

Despite sluggish sales, Southern California home prices remain near record highs.

The median home price reached $815,000 in July, the fourth-highest figure ever recorded in the region and just 2% below its all-time peak.

Those prices have made homeownership unattainable for the vast majority of households.

According to the California Association of Realtors, just 15% of households in Orange County could afford to purchase a home this past spring. The figure was 17% in Los Angeles and San Diego counties, 19% in Ventura County, 28% in Riverside County and 34% in San Bernardino County.

There has been some relief in the pace of price increases. Since 2023, home values across Southern California have grown by approximately 2% annually, a significant slowdown from the 7% average annual increase recorded during the previous decade.

But that trend presents another challenge for the housing market. Buyers who once viewed real estate as an investment that would rapidly appreciate may now be less willing to make such a costly commitment.

Beyond the purchase price, the cost of maintaining a mortgage has become another major obstacle.

A Southern California buyer purchasing a median-priced home would face an estimated monthly housing payment of $5,765, including mortgage payments, property taxes, homeowners insurance and mortgage insurance.

That’s a 72% increase over five years.

The Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates beginning in 2022 contributed to the surge in borrowing costs, following several years when mortgage rates had fallen to historic lows.

And the monthly payment isn’t the only financial hurdle. Buyers would also need approximately $81,500 upfront for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home.

Renting, meanwhile, remains considerably cheaper.

Zillow estimates show that the typical monthly rent for a house or apartment in Southern California was approximately $2,860 in July, less than half the estimated monthly cost of purchasing a home.

Mortgage rates have also added to the pressure. The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage stood at 6.5% in July before climbing to 7.3% by mid-October.

That increase alone reduced prospective buyers’ purchasing power by roughly 8%, making an already expensive housing market even more difficult to enter.
